utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I immediately offer my apologies and a not very satisfactory but I'm afraid extremely simple explanation which is that my watch at the moment, Your Honour, after performing admirably for three years, shows the time right now as one minute to 9.00 and I'm afraid that, having gone by my own watch which has chosen this morning to pack up on me to that extent, I simply had no idea, Your Honour that I wasn't coming to court on time in the normal way. I realise that that's very inconvenient to all concerned, I apologise to everybody inconvenienced. There is no more I can say, Your Honour. That's what's happened. I will, of course, change my watch at the earliest opportunity now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Stewart, if it doesn't happen any more than once every one and a half year, then the Court is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I am grateful, Your Honour. And I shall try to preserve that average, or better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The same is granted to the Prosecution. Then are you ready to continue the examination of Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Trbojevic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Your Honour, I wonder if I could just ask somebody to give me assistance. I've had this problem in this court: I'm afraid I don't know where the power point is. It's not in such an obvious place in this court. Down here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're excused for an absence of a couple of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: While I go subterranean for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no luck, Your Honour, I'm afraid. I'm sure while we're proceeding if somebody just comes in and shows me where this point is, then we'll have lift-off in a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that someone will come and assist you. Mr. Trbojevic, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony and I'd also like to remind you that if any question is put to you of which you think that answering would incriminate yourself, that you may object to doing so, and as I said yesterday, the Court will then decide whether it will compel you to answer that question, in which case the answer could not be used against you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trbojevic. I'd like to turn first to a meeting of the Council for National Security in the government which was held on April 24th, 1992 and which is found behind tab 2 in binder 1. Mr. Trbojevic, while that -- while the minutes of that meeting are being produced for you, I'd indicate that I'm going to draw your attention to a decision that appears as the third to last before the rulings section of the minutes, and that was the following: "A decision was passed stating that the exchange of prisoners be handled by the Ministry of Justice after the internal affairs organs finish their work." Now, Mr. Trbojevic, I recognise that this preceded your entry into government by approximately one month; nevertheless, I want to ask you if you can tell us first what work of the internal affairs organs was contemplated by that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you have said yourself, I don't know when this was passed. I did not participate in formulating this document, but based on the formulation itself, one can conclude that if there are some persons who had been detained, that it was the police organs who were supposed to interview or question them first to see whether they were of any interest to the police organs before these people were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And thereafter, that is, upon completion of the efforts of the organs of internal affairs, the Ministry of Justice would be responsible for effecting the exchange; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that and I didn't know that this fell under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice. There was no information regarding what was being done on that issue. I know that there existed a Commission for Exchange; however, I did not consider it to be an organ of the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who did you consider to be responsible for the work of the Commission of Exchange?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that that was a commission which was attached to the military organs. It was logical that there were some prisoners after military operations, and the issue of whether these persons would be detained or exchanged or released is something that logically ought to fall under the jurisdiction of military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the decision of the Council for National Security and the government on April 24th that the Ministry of Justice would be responsible or would handle the exchange of prisoners after the internal affairs organs had finished their work comes as a surprise to you, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Entirely. As far as I know, the Ministry of Justice did not have the functional ability to deal with this. It did not have staff that could have managed that. And based on my personal experience, I know nothing about the activities of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not the work of the commission was the subject of attention in government sessions in which you were involved after your arrival in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must confess that I do not remember. It is possible that that was mentioned, but as for the government taking position as to how that was supposed to function, as to government deciding, issuing criteria as to who ought to be exchanged and who oughtn't -- should not, I don't think that anything was done on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned during the course of an answer your conclusion that it was logical that there are some prisoners after military operations. Do you recall that the issue of prisoners held by Bosnian Serb authorities, beginning in the period early May and extending on through the rest of the year, was the subject of allegations by the international community that those prisoners were the victims of forcible population displacements of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first information I received regarding that had to do with the arrival of Mr. Mazowiecki in Banja Luka. That was in the summer of 1992, I'm not sure exactly when. I know that his arrival and his visit to Banja Luka, Manjaca and Prijedor were given quite a lot of publicity and it was then that a lot of that information same to surface. That was the first I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look next at an article contained at tab 51, which I believe is the first tab in binder 2. Mr. Trbojevic, tab 51 contains an article by the Reuters news service from May 12th, 1992, reflecting the remarks of a special envoy for the UN's High Commissioner for Refugees, who said, among others things in the article: "I thought I had seen everything, but what is happening in Bosnia passes all imagination. What we are seeing is something like World War II with population centres being destroyed and towns and villages attacked not as military objects but with the sole purpose of driving the people away." He said this at a news conference and he said further, "The difference from other conflicts I have seen is that, in Bosnia, the creation of a legion of displaced persons is not the consequence of military action but the aim of it." Further on in the press conference, he identifies some numbers of displaced persons and so on. First of all, were you familiar with allegations -- with the specific allegations by UNHCR representative or with more general allegations at that time by representatives of the international community or international media that population centres were being attacked and civilians driven off?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, I was in Sarajevo. My son was arrested in the street and beaten up. I had no idea about these matters that are being discussed here. There's a complete analysis here about the causes and effects, and it would be absurd for me to give my position regarding that. At that time, I was just a citizen in Sarajevo trying to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, would you please answer the questions, because you said a lot of words --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Pale, did you learn from Mr. Djeric or from other members of the Bosnian Serb authorities that such allegations were being made by the international community?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody briefed me on the situation, if that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I actually have something broader in mind. Irrespective of whether you were formally briefed on this by any of those officials, were you told in conversations or did you learn from other sources, once you arrived in Pale, that such allegations were being made and were the subject of concern by Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would you turn next to tab 52. Mr. Trbojevic, as you can see, tab 52 contains a letter from Prime Minister Branko Djeric sent to the United States Secretary of State James Baker on May 24th, 1992. In that letter, Mr. Djeric assures Mr. Baker that the Serbian side is holding no hostages, operating no concentration camps, and is not killing unarmed civilians in Bosnia. Then he mentions the reports alleging such crimes appearing in the U.S. press and elsewhere are not based upon facts. Do you know, sir, what reports from the United States and elsewhere Mr. Djeric was referring to in this letter to Mr. Baker?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe that he wrote this bona fide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm afraid you'll have to explain that a little further, precisely what you mean by "bona fide."

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was fully convinced of what he stated in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My question actually was whether or not you can tell us what reports he was referring to in the U.S. press and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, Mr. Djeric refers to the most disturbing news about decisions of the ministerial council suggesting the possible use of force would flow against the Bosnian Serbs. Were you aware of that most disturbing news emanating from the ministerial conference?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could I put a few questions to the witness. You said, Mr. Trbojevic, that you are fully convinced that what Mr. Djeric stated in his letter was correct. Why -- on the basis of what did you gain that conviction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I thought that Djeric wrote this, fully convinced that it was true. We did not have at our disposal -- I did not know that he had at his disposal any information to the effect that the Serb forces had camps in which they created unbearable conditions for the inmates, that they were conducting ethnic cleansing of large territories. We had no such information at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis of the allegations he describes, to what extent was it investigated at that time whether such situations did exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not natural for an institution such as the government to know nothing about what is going on around it. It was expected that the police or the military would supply some reports with information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question, Mr. Trbojevic. My question was: On the basis of the allegations made, what investigations were made in order to come to the conclusion, as you said, that Mr. Djeric could write this letter fully convinced of the correctness of the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that a commission was established, the commission was supposed to go to Krajina and to report on what was going on there. However, we did not receive the report of that commission. The General Staff, in its report to the Supreme Command, whether the General Staff ever informed the Supreme Command of that, I really don't know about that. I did not see any police reports either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say the commission was established. When was that commission established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime during the summer. The information could probably be found in documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The letter was written on the 24th of May. You told us that Mr. Djeric, while sending this letter, would be convinced of the truthfulness of it. I asked you what investigations were made to find out whether these allegations were true or not true, and then of course I mean to say when these allegations were made, and that, in view of the letter of May 24th, should have been before the 24th of May. What investigations were done, not somewhere in the summer, but prior to writing this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What makes you believe that Mr. Djeric was convinced that what he wrote was correct if no investigations you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believed him that he had no information regarding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He received no information. I also understand that on the allegations, you are not aware of any investigation being made to see what was true about these allegations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just told us that you are not aware of any investigations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that I knew that a group was supposed to go to Krajina to -- for a fact-finding mission and then report on the situation there, but I know of no other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, the question: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might have been in the course of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as I said to you earlier, I'm interested to know what was done in relation to the allegations made prior to writing a letter on the 24th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've stated several times that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I'm coming back to my first question now. What's the basis -- you just say, "I believed Mr. Djeric had no information since no investigation took place. He must have been convinced that this was the truth."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that I believed him when he said that he didn't know anything about it and I did not know of any information that would prove to the contrary. That's why I believed him Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. when he said that he knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Now that commission that was to be sent to Krajina, when was that established? You said somewhere in June; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly but there's a document that I signed containing an order to the effect that this should be looked into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is that commission on which you just said that you never received a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you do when you did not receive any report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This commission was supposed to be a commission under the Ministry of Justice, and of course we believed that a report would eventually be submitted. However, the events then took their course and there was no more need for such a report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why was there no further need for such a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information about the events at Manjaca and at Omarska became, so to say, general knowledge to a higher or lesser degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there was no need to know further details for the government because it had been in the press already; is that how I have to understand your answer that there was no need for such a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no need to insist on the report being submitted because the events became general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, did Mr. Djeric consider these reports from the U.S. and others to be simply anti-Serb propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not analyse these things item-by-item but it is well known that there was an anti-Serb propaganda going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Djeric consider information from the UNHCR, from the United States government, from the international media -- well, let me put that to you again -- governmental sources to be part of that anti-Serb propaganda campaign you're alluding to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which documents he had in mind, he had within reach and which were the documents on the basis of which he formed his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you consider these reports to be part of an anti-Serb propaganda campaign?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw them, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I turn your attention to page 59 of the May interview that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor. That would be page 48 of the B/C/S. If the witness could be presented with page 48 of the B/C/S. Mr. Trbojevic, at that portion of the interview, the letter from Mr. Djeric is being addressed, the 24 May 1992 letter. And you stated, and that can be found in your second comment on page 59 of the English translation: "So the alleged report about things happening in the American press are not based on the facts. I don't know when did the first report show up. Now I know that the most of these reports were false, and you know that better than I do. It was part of the propaganda which was malicious towards the Serb nation." And again, Mr. Trbojevic, is that your view of the reports coming from the United States and elsewhere that were the subject of Mr. Djeric's letter to Mr. Baker?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You seem to be constructing something here, concocting something. I was saying that news reports were formed to be in the function of something, but I'm not referring to a government. I say that I know now that many of these news reports were false, and I'm referring to newspaper articles, and I adhere to that view today. None of the government positions or official documents issued by any organisation, I never saw any of them and I did not give my opinion in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, did you come to understand that the possibility, as discussed at the ministerial conference in Lisbon, that force would be used against the Bosnian Serbs arose in part from reports of the type we looked at a bit earlier from UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the peace-making process that consisted of the Cutileiro Plan was taking place in Lisbon, then of course I can say that I had some information originating from the people involved in that process which had to do with the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the relations between the warring parties. I had some information about that that I heard from the people forming the negotiating team. But as far as the possibility of a bombing attack or anything of that sort, I did not have any information about that or about any such -- about what these threats consisted of in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm simply asking whether you understood that the information available to the members of the ministerial conference or to Mr. Baker or to other governments consisted of more than newspaper articles but consisted of information from various sources, including the type we looked at earlier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not really look into whether the information was based on some sort of a document. I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next to tab 109, which is found in binder 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you are often referring to the March and May interviews and it seems that there are two copies circulating, one with a paging which is quite different from the other. So it seems that you are not working from the copy that you provided to the Registry. When you just referred to, I think it was page 59, it seems that that is page 59 of a copy which is available to the Judges but is not the copy that has been provided to the Registry. So I wonder whether it would not be better to give the Registry the same because there might be a moment that someone would like to check what was said on the basis of the transcript and then it will create huge problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand. I will do so, Your Honour. I apologise for that. That copy rose out of an attempt to correlate the English and B/C/S transcripts so I could refer immediately to them but that effort was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You solved one problem but you created another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just mention, Your Honour - I'm not quite sure whether this is the same problem or linked to it - but the -- there is a continuous document of both interviews, numbered 1 to 100 and whatever it is, and then there are the two interviews numbered separately. Now I - and I'm not scoring a point here, Your Honour - but I and some people within the Prosecution team have worked from the continuous copy. Mr. Tieger and I have discussed that. We came to the conclusion the simple solution was that if I simply added 50 to every number when we were dealing with the second interview, that would work. Unfortunately, it doesn't, so if I could inform Mr. Tieger because the discrepancy is 56 pages and it's not consistent either. So the request is only that when referring to these pages, if Mr. Tieger could just give those few extra seconds while those of us working from completely different numbering can locate the passage, that would solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There should be no confusion, that's the only thing the parties should take care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention another problem which is that the -- in some ways I was slightly comforted by the fact that the extremely efficient technical staff took quite a few minutes even to locate a suitable power point in this court, but having located it, I notice that for some reason or other it's not working, with the result that my computer ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, at least I see a power point, I know that we are going to break our legs, but what I understand from laptops, they will function for some time even without plugging them in. I see it from here at least as a temporary solution, or it's too far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, no, that's entirely right. I was going to say, first of all, I can use this power point. It's not entirely safe, I'm just making a request that at some point the technical staff could enable me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do that -- if you do that during the break, then we'll miss no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, I do have a point, Your Honour, which is this: I also need about 30 seconds because my computer has now hibernated and I need to plug it in and get it up and running again, Your Honour, before I can proceed, so I'm just going to need 30 seconds, please, to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. It should be all right, Your Honour, but it's just got to restart itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps during the next break, Mr. Stewart, you should ask yourself why you need one minute to ask for 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not regard that as a fair remark at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, tab 109 contains agreement number 2, which was signed on May 23rd, 1992 in the meeting in Geneva which was held to discuss the implementation of the agreement of 22 May and which included, as -- among its provisions, 2A, exchange list of prisoners and take the necessary steps with a view to the release of prisoners. We can see toward the top of the page the representatives in attendance at the meeting who participated in the agreement and who signed the agreement, including Mr. D. Kalinic, representative of Mr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the Serbian Democratic Party. First of all, is that a reference to Dr. Dragan Kalinic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And he was the minister of health of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. -- or Dr. Kalinic was a member of government; in fact, as a minister of health, a high-ranking member of the Bosnian Serb government, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What necessary steps to release prisoners was contemplated by this agreement, according to Dr. Kalinic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Kalinic report back to the government or to other representatives of the Bosnian Serb authorities about the agreement and about the undertakings contemplated by the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I believe he informed Dr. Karadzic, but I'm not sure whether this applies to the whole of the government. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this applies to the circumstances of prisoners being held by the Bosnian Serb forces and authorities, at least in part; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the issue of the circumstances of prisoners who were held by Bosnian Serb forces a matter of concern of the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the accurate data about the numbers of such persons and the conditions under which they were detained were not in government's possession, and since one could not even assume that these circumstances would be so excessive as they were, one did not really -- was not really concerned about it in that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Kalinic report concerns by the ICRC that the conditions under which prisoners were held were a matter of concern?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically whether this was done and what way it was done, but I do know that there wasn't a special government session that was dedicated to this issue, and I know that no conclusions were adopted with a view to remedying the situation. That's why I'm inclined to believe that the government was not provided with a full report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask one clarification. You said that's why you are inclined to believe that the government was not provided with a full report. "Full report" by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By Dr. Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know to whom Dr. Kalinic met or to whom Dr. Kalinic reported or with whom he met after returning from Geneva?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that he went there as a representative of Dr. Radovan Karadzic. He was in touch with him very frequently. Now, whether he went to see him on his return from Geneva, I can't really vouch for that particular period, but I do know that he was in touch with him frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, let me ask you to look quickly at a document contained behind tab 74 in binder 2. Now, Mr. Trbojevic, this document is a list of approximately 400 persons who were taken from Bratunac to Pale and ultimately on to Visoko and were held in Pale from May 14th through 17th. First of all, given your knowledge of the geography and layout and population of Pale in May of 1992, would it have been possible for a group of that size to be brought in to Pale on a secret or unknown basis or would everyone have known about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pale is a small town and the arrival of a group of people numbering -- how many people did you say there were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the arrival of 400 persons would not have passed unnoticed. I don't know where they were put up and for how long. I don't know what had been done with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You arrived in Pale within days of this event; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about it from other members of the government or the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not these persons were transferred from Bratunac and then taken to Muslim territory was pursuant to efforts by any organ of the government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know anything about this operation. I have no idea who issued orders or why or what was the aim of it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at page 3 of the document, I believe that's both in the B/C/S and the English versions. There we see a signature by Mr. S. Markovic above the writing "Member of the Government's Commission on Behalf of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior for the Exchange of Prisoners of War." What can you tell us about Mr. Markovic and the government's Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. I don't know when the commission was appointed. I do not know Markovic. It is possible that I met him somewhere, but I don't know him, nor do I know his post -- position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document that was previously introduced into evidence. That's P436, and that can be found in tab 73, Your Honours. That's a decision dated the 8th of May, 1992 and it's headed "Decision to Form a Central Commission," and signed by Professor Djeric as Prime Minister. First of all, Mr. Trbojevic, do you see the name of Slobodan Markovic, the representative of the Ministry of the Interior as a -- named as a member of the central commission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, does that shed any further light for you on who Mr. Markovic was and what his function in the government was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is of no assistance to me. I don't know the man. I don't know what he did. I can see that he was a member of the commission but that doesn't trigger my memory. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Item number one, it indicates that the central commission is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hereby appointed and it's described as the "Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War, Arrested Persons, and the Bodies of Those Killed." What's the difference between prisoners of war and arrested persons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arrested persons, as it stated here, is a term used in law to denote persons detained based on a decision of an organ. Based on that decision, they are deprived of their liberty. As for the prisoners of war, those persons were taken prisoner in the course of military operation. As for the bodies of those killed, I believe that is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And which organ of the government had authority to arrest people in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He didn't say organ of the government, he said organ. Mr. Tieger's introduced that extra word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which organ or body in Republika Srpska had the authority to arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person can be deprived of their liberty by police in the course of police activities. They are convicted and sentenced by courts. And in addition to that, all of these actions can be carried out by the organs of the military police. As for the prisoners of war, I'm no expert for the laws of war; however, I think that this applies to persons who were deprived of their liberty in the course of war operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you remind me what your position was at the time the central commission was established, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I was not present in Pale, not yet. When I arrived in Pale, I became Deputy Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 14th of May -- let me repeat my question: On the 8th of May, the beginning of the month of May, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 14th of May, I was still living in Sarajevo and working as an attorney. On the 17th of May, I was arrested. On the 20th of May, I left Sarajevo and arrived in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were deputy minister. At what date were you deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Officially, I think on the 8th of June; however, Prime Minister Djeric told me that this is how it would be and I was by his side starting on the 22nd or 23rd of May, observing what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber wondered whether it made much sense to go through all the, I would say, normal powers whereas this case, at least that's the provisional impression, is not about the exercise of normal police powers necessarily. At least the scale on which people were detained at least give a different impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, although my question -- I'm sorry that it wasn't clear -- was more directed at who was the subject of the reference in the document or which body was the subject of a reference rather than the powers under law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you made the distinction. But then it took the course of explaining what -- who had powers to arrest and further details might not be of great assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, and I think there might have been a more expeditious way of eliciting that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, before we move on to the next document, I just want to direct your attention to the first name -- first member named on the commission, and are you able to make out the name of that person who was a representative of the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here Rajko Colovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tieger come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could we turn next to tab 19, the 24th session of the government, held on the 9th of June, 1992. Tab 19 in binder 1. Mr. Trbojevic, tab 19 contains the minutes of the session of the government held on June 9th, 1992, the day after your formal appointment as deputy minister, I believe, although the minutes indicate you were not present at this particular meeting. But I'm wondering if you can direct your attention to agenda item 1 that refers first to the government's support for the order of the Central Committee for the Exchange of Prisoners, and B, correspondence from the president of the Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners, and then a conclusion that the ministers should talk to Rajko Colovic to determine what are the motives for requesting the change, and if the reasons are justified, do the work of the committee president until a new president can be appointed. Can you tell us what was happening with the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners at that time, and in particular with Mr. Colovic's request for change.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Rajko Colovic. I knew him even before I arrived in Pale. Even nowadays, he's still a colleague of mine in the justice system. I didn't even know that he was a member of the commission and that he asked to be relieved of his duties. We never talked about that. Therefore, I don't know what ever caused him to ask to be relieved of duties. It says here the government supports the order. It says that the Prime Minister will talk to the president of the commission to see why he's asking to be replaced. It is stated here that we ought to apply both international and domestic regulations, so based on the text, I really don't know what I could comment here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, if you do not know anything about it, there's no need to read the text because that's what the Chamber can do itself as well. Mr. Tieger, please proceed. Yes, it's 10.30 anyhow. Mr. Trbojevic, you are invited to directly answer the questions, and if you are not asked whether you knew Mr. Colovic or not, then refrain from telling us matters that you are not asked. If you do not know anything about it, then you say, "I've got no idea why he wanted to resign," and if there is any additional question, Mr. Tieger will ask it. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Tieger, perhaps a few practical matters. First of all, protective measures in respect of witnesses 31 and 73, I think we are still waiting for a response by the Defence. It was the -- the response was due the 25th of March. If you just now write it down, Mr. Stewart, and let me know if my information is wrong, and otherwise provide us with the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I certainly don't have any basis for suggesting it's wrong, Your Honours, so I've written down the numbers and will inquire during the next break, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there is some supplementary information provided by the OTP in view of protective measures of a 92 bis witness -- of the 92 bis witnesses in general and I think we do not know whether we have to expect any further responses to that. If not, if you'd like to do that, the Chamber would like to receive it by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll do exactly the same with that as I am with the other points. I'll follow it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there is another issue but I'd rather not deal with it in the presence of the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, before we move on, as you were being escorted to the witness box by the usher, you may have overheard Mr. Stewart and I mentioning your name and coming to learn that I'm mispronouncing your name. I apologise for that. I don't expect it to get better but I recognise that I'm not pronouncing your name properly, and my apologies for that. Can we next turn, then, to tab 20, please, in binder 1. Now, tab 20 reflects or contains the minutes of a -- of the 25th government session of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 10th of June, 1992. Again, Mr. Trbojevic, I note that the minutes reflect that you were absent. This meeting takes place the day after the session we looked at just before the recess, at which the government concluded that the treatment and exchange of prisoners is a responsible and complex issue. At this session on the 10th of June, if you'll look at page 3 -- well, it's page 3 of the English and it's immediately under agenda item 7. The government concluded that the Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners and that this report should pay special attention on treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera. The report would be considered by the government after which it would be submitted to the Presidency of the Republic. Mr. Trbojevic, can you tell us what information was available to the government that prompted the conclusion that the Ministry of Justice should be tasked with preparing a report about prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about it perhaps not exactly, Mr. Trbojevic, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have no information, no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, did you receive the minutes of the government meetings, even if you were not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most likely the minutes were copied, but as to whether they reached my hands, I couldn't tell you. I probably received some minutes but didn't receive all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you receive any preparatory documents for those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether a report was prepared, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether it was discussed at a government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were members of the government or other officials among the Bosnian Serb authorities at that time discussing the general issue of the treatment of civilian populations and prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next then to tab 23, the government session of June 15th. Now, Mr. Trbojevic, the minutes reflect that you were the chair of the meeting that was held on June 15th. Let me ask you to turn, please, to agenda item 10. That's found on page 4 of the English translation. Agenda item 10, Mr. Trbojevic, reflects the following: "The government has considered the proposed report. It has been concluded that the issue of prisoners exchange is extremely important, complex, and delicate and that if sufficient attention is not paid to it, it can cause a number of negative consequences for the whole republic. It has been agreed that working group consisting of professor Branko Djeric, Milan Trbojevic, Dr. Dragan Kalinic, Mico Stanisic, Bogdan Subotic and Momcilo Mandic should consider all the aspects of the prisoner exchange problem and that they should propose systematic and other solutions, taking into account our and international regulations. It is obvious that solving this problem is urgent and that the regulations and concrete measures for solving of this issue should be proposed as soon as possible." First of all, Mr. Trbojevic, is the proposed report which was considered by the government on June 15th the report that was referred to in the minutes we looked at earlier, that is, the report that the Ministry of Justice was tasked to produce about prisoners on the 10th of June?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty. It is possible, but I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other proposed report on the issue of prisoners other than the one that the government tasked justice to produce and that was reflected in the June 10th minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Based on the report, the government concluded that the issue of prisoners was, among other things, "... complex and delicate and can cause a number of negative consequences for the whole republic." What information was contained in that report that indicated the complex, delicate and potentially adverse impact of the issue of prisoners exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the text of that report. I don't know what it said. I assume that the report can be found among other documents but I couldn't quote any of its portions now or give my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wouldn't ask you to actually quote from the report after this length of time, but this was the first session of the government that you chaired, wasn't it, Mr. Trbojevic, or at least among the first sessions that you chaired?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you were actually the chair of the meeting at June 13th as well. At this meeting, the government considered an issue that was extremely important, by its own conclusions, and that could lead to a number of negative consequences for the whole republic. So as a general matter, what information was discussed at that meeting that was so important and so potentially adverse?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber finds reason to warn you that you are under a duty to tell the truth. As the solemn declaration said, the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And I'm putting to you the consequences that may result from a failure to do so. If you do not speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, the maximum penalty for false testimony under solemn declaration is a fine of 100.000 euros or a term of imprisonment of 7 years or both. This is a formal warning under Rule 91 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I'm seeking from you any information you have about the nature of the discussion that took place on June 15th at this government session concerning an issue that was regarded by the government and members of the government itself as extremely important and that was considered to have potentially adverse consequences to the republic. What can you tell me about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fully conscious of the oath that I took. It is just that I do not recall. There is no trace in my memory of the text submitted by somebody and the problems that the text pointed out to. Naturally, I can interpret some things, because over the years a certain amount of information was collected; however, from that period of time, May/June 1992, I really couldn't tell you anything more about that. I saw the report signed by Momcilo Mandic, Stanisic, and the report stated that there were many prisoners of war, many arrested and so on, but I couldn't confirm that because there's no trace of that text left in my memory. Naturally, this is an issue that had to be regulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you said, "I saw the report signed by Momcilo Mandic and Stanisic and the report stated that there were many prisoners of war, many arrested and so on ..." Did the report confine itself to establishing that there were many prisoners of war and arrested persons or did it say more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've said that I am Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. unable to state that I laid my eyes on such a report. It says here that somebody submitted a report. I don't know who it was who submitted it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I'm not asking who submitted it. I was just reading the transcript of your testimony. And if you say that that's not what you said, then we'll check that on the basis of the original tape in Bosnian Croatian Serbian. You said, "I saw the report signed by Momcilo Mandic, Stanisic." Is that correct? If you didn't say that, then we'll have that checked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that I cannot say that I did see the report submitted by either the president of the Commission for the Exchange or by Momcilo Mandic or by Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you were chairing a meeting in which, as a chairperson, at least you were involved in a conversation saying that the government has considered the proposed report and has drawn conclusions about the importance. What do you know about the report? Do you know that it existed, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe that -- while I'm fully endorsing, with respect, Your Honour's proposal that the B/C/S tape should be checked, might I respectfully suggest that that should be done straight away before we proceed further so that -- there was -- when one looks at the whole answer, it does cry out for some checking, as Your Honour suggests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid that we could ask Madam Registrar to -- I take it that we have to wait until the end of this -- we can't copy anything from the tape unless the tape is finished. Is that correct, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll change the tapes and have a look at what has been said at what appears on my computer as 11.14 and then especially the line reading "I saw the report signed by Momcilo Mandic, Stanisic," which is at 11.14.19 -- no, 11.14.25, and including the next line 11.14.30, and the next line 11.14.41. We all have to stop speaking until we get the information that a new tape is put in place. Mr. Tieger, we can proceed at this moment with the examination, although cueing up the tape that has been removed now will take a couple of more minutes, so we'll return to that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I mention that I have -- and it's nothing to do with my watch, Your Honour, but I have 11.17.46 for that reference whereas Your Honour apparently had 11.14.25. I have no idea why there should be such a discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you have as the time on your computer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where it says, "I saw the report --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you on the very bottom of the -- in the right down corner, what time do you have there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour, I see. I have 11.28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your computer has a bit of a different time from mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I should say Your Honour, I'm not talking about my computer here, I'm talking about the court-provided computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The computer you are using.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The one I'm using, Your Honour, yes, just to clarify because my computer has had its issues this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, we could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could that be fixed? This is obviously potentially very inconvenient. Not right now, but sometimes synchronisation is important here because certain -- if we get these discrepancies they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can always adapt the clock time of your computer if you want to, Mr. Stewart. That's basics in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can with my own, Your Honour, yes, of course I can. I know how to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is just the laptop. Yes, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand the court has asked me to continue, although I wasn't the one who asked for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm aware of that, but what I would say is that we could not immediately at this moment take up the issue we got stuck in, so if there's anything else, otherwise we have to wait for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would suggest that we wait because I think it would pointless to sort of move around that issue which is now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps Judge Hanoteau has one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to take advantage of this brief suspension to ask a question to the witness. When the witness was appointed as a minister, what position did he take? What was his role? I think that this was not clearly defined. You said that you were not given a specific position, a specific mandate because you were Deputy Prime Minister. What was your role, what was your task? You were talking to the Prime Minister but I would like to know what task you were performing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Formally, there were several Deputy Prime Ministers. I was supposed to exercise the position of the Deputy Prime Minister for the Interior. There was one for the economy, another one for finances, and I was supposed to deal with internal affairs, home affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please elaborate on your role. "Home affairs," what do you mean by this? What did it consist of? What was your task, what was your relation with the home minister, what meetings did you attend, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to make my answers as concise as possible but if you're asking me to explain, then the -- this is the substance of it: The Prime Minister for internal policies, to say, was someone who was supposed to be the immediate superior to the minister of the interior and the minister of justice, dealing with the organisation of state administration and the functioning of justice administration. This is something that was supposed to be dealt with by the relevant ministers. I have given a detailed explanation of this in my earlier statements. From the very beginning this government started to operate some conflicts arose where the ministers of justice and internal affairs felt that they were under an investigation launched by the Prime Minister and myself over abuses. So that there was this relationship of friction which was characterised by an almost absolute absence of communication between, on the one hand, the minister of the interior and the minister of justice, and on the other, the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean by "abuses"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some warehouses of certain companies were being mentioned which, at the beginning of war operations, fell on the Serb-controlled side and it was suspected that the goods contained in these warehouses had been stolen with the assistance of some police officers under the auspices of these two ministers. This investigation was never carried out fully and the suspicions were not confirmed but this caused them -- these two ministers to be indignant over this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the minister of the interior and the minister of justice? Did you have to -- did you ask them to provide you with some reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We set up a commission and we called them for some interviews, asking them to give their statement about the matter, which they naturally declined. Next, Branko Djeric tried to eliminate them from the government through a reshuffling process, and since this did not work out, this sort of situation prevailed until the month of October, when Djeric resigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, would you please carefully listen to the part of your testimony of this morning we'll play to you at this very moment. And could I invite the interpreters to pay specific attention to the words spoken, and Interpreter, if there is any word unclear or if it could be not well understood, I'd like to be informed. Could the technical booth please play the relevant portion of the B/C/S tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This problem was raised. I cannot now interpret the situation because a lot of time has elapsed since the information were -- was being collected, but from the period in May and June I cannot tell you that I saw the report that had been signed by either the president of the commission for the exchange or by Momcilo Mandic as the minister of justice or by Mico Stanisic. This -- and say this report says that there are many prisoners, many people detained. I cannot tell you this because I do not have this text in my mind, to be frank. That it was necessary to regulate this issue that ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think a sufficient part has been played. Mr. Trbojevic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it should be placed on record, the witness was correct in what he said about that. The -- what's being played back does confirm what he subsequently said, because it's significantly different from what appeared on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear to me. I was looking at it, I didn't listen to the English translation, but I take it that finally we could establish with the support of the interpreters that the witness said that he cannot tell us that he saw the report that had been signed by either the president of the commission for the exchange or by Momcilo Mandic as the minister of justice or by Mico Stanisic. Mr. Trbojevic, you are perfectly right that the transcript gave a wrong impression of what you said and that was -- explains perhaps why I was so insistent. And thanks to the technical facilities, we can clarify these issues. If you have felt uncomfortable with it, I apologise for it to happen. I would have, however, a few more questions on it, and that's the following: So a report, even if you have not seen it, was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is what the document here says, then there's no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this report, because you earlier said that a report on detention facilities was asked for but it was never received, do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that report that was never received, was that another report? Because this report, as I understand, seems to have been received even though not read by you. I'm just seeking clarification of your earlier answer where you said that a report was asked for but never received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that there was one report which was submitted by Mr. Slobodan Avlijas, and I know that this report never reached the government but I learned about all of this many years later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I cannot really be precise in determining which report is the one we have before us here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You earlier talked about a commission to be sent to Krajina. Who was heading that commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know at this time. I believe that the Prosecutor showed me a decision that I signed saying that a commission was supposed to go to Krajina and I believe the names of the persons are mentioned therein and you can find it out there, or perhaps it said that the Ministry of Justice was to designate who was to go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that was at a different occasion, was not the report or committee or whatever discussed at this meeting of the 15th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the 15th of June minutes tell us that you were -- that it was agreed that you would be among the members of a working group on the issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This working group here never met, in part because of the hostility that existed between Stanisic and Mandic on the one hand, and Djeric and me on the other, and in part, also, because the minister of defence thought it fell under his jurisdiction to deal with prisoners and orders related to them as well as about the matters concerning their treatment. That's why I believe he was dealing with these issues. This commission, however, did not meet at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there ever a report saying that the commission or the working group could not function or could not do what it had to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you regret that this commission or this working group could not do what it was tasked with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no -- there was no information available that would indicate that the situation was terrible, horrible, and that something had to be done about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer to my question. My question was not whether there were any reasons to investigate but whether you did regret that the task given to this working group was not fulfilled by it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to explain to you that at the time none of us were aware of the need for such a task to be carried out let alone of the significance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At a later stage, of course, everyone regretted it, but when we're talking about that specific period, there was no need to regret something that we were not aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you regretted what happened in these detention facilities, I'm asking you whether you regretted that finally the work this working group was tasked with was not done; that is, to consider all the aspects of prisoner exchange problems, to propose systematic and other solutions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that we did not regret that fact, and I've tried to explain why we felt that way about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you are telling us is that the government considered this to be an urgent problem that should be dealt with without any further delay, and if I ask you about your feelings about this task not being fulfilled, you say, "Well, as a matter of fact, there was no urgent problem, there was nothing to consider at all," which is totally inconsistent with the decision taken by the government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, there were exchange commissions within each core. In each region, exchanges were carried out. So we believed that the system was functioning. Yes, there were problems, there were many people detained. We had to provide all the necessary conditions for them - the food, the sanitary needs and so on - however, we believed that things were developing and that the problem would be solved through exchanges. It occurred to no one that this would turn into a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "We had to provide all the necessary conditions for them - the food, the sanitary needs ..." Who do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, listen, those who kept people in detention had to feed them and provide water for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but was that any of your business at the government level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government most likely had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. contacts with the Ministry of Commerce, and the Bureau for Commodities most likely provided some supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking back, on the basis of the information you have now, would you consider the condition in detention facilities in terms of food and sanitary needs satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had we been able to have any hints about the actual situation, I'm sure that the following government session would have been scheduled to be held in Omarska in order to go to the site and to see right there what could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the working group had done what it had been tasked with, if the matter would have been further investigated, would you agree with me that there would have been a fair chance that the conditions had become known to the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. I have said that I didn't know what this information was about. As for the other report that I had opportunity to see several times later, I came to the conclusion that even this report did not inform about the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, again the question: Having established that you had -- that there would have been a fair chance had the conditions become known to the government, do you regret that the committee for -- or the working group did not do what it was tasked with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do regret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your testimony well that if the work had been done the government considered at that moment urgent and important, that the chance that the conditions in the detention facilities would be known in due time to the government was a fair chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider it a failure that finally the government, at least as far as your knowledge goes, was not informed about the conditions in the camps, in the detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do consider that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a question I'd like to ask. You stated that you had learned later on that a report had been submitted by Slobodan Avlijas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was Slobodan Avlijas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was an inspector for penitentiary institutions under the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you read this report afterwards or did you -- were you informed of -- about this report afterwards? What was in that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a description of a camp where certain people were held who had satisfactory food supplies, who had medical assistance, sanitary conditions were provided for them as well, and this site did not resemble a criminal institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you said, sir, that this report, once it was drafted, was not handed over to the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was this report given to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned about that much, much later. And based on what I learned, it was submitted to the minister of justice who, in turn, transmitted it, allegedly, to Mr. Karadzic. This is the information I received from Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this should have been handed over to the head of government, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. Naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this was not the case; it was handed over directly to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, you have to be even more patient. Judge Canivell has a question too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to know whether you could -- which camp was mentioned in the report which was not handed over at a latter stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the information mentioned in the minutes of the government session or do you mean the report prepared by Slobodan Avlijas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, neither of the two. At one stage, you stated that this report was drafted by an inspector - I don't remember the name of this inspector - and this referred to a camp where a number of people had been well treated, well fed, well looked after. Which camp is this; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you're referring to this bit that pertained to the report of Slobodan Avlijas, and this report dealt with the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It occurs to me that in light of the Court's questions, rather than ask the questions that I was immediately -- that were immediately going to follow, I thought I'd distribute the tab 100, which -- in tab 100 of your binders, there is a cover page but the document is not contained. This is the document. It's the report that's been referred to, or at least we'll check with the witness that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 100 is in binder 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whoever would miss tab 102, I've got them double, so if there's anyone -- I know that we are talking about 100, but I see that I've got two times 102. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And at the same time, Your Honour, it might be best if I also directed the Court's attention to tab 92, which contains a report dated August 22, 1992, by Mr. Avlijas and Mr. Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trbojevic, I'm directing your attention to both reports, both the report of August 22, 1992 by Mr. Avlijas and Mr. Saric and the report of October 22nd, 1992. And if you could look those two reports over and tell us first whether or not either one of those is a report you were referring to in responding to the questions of Judge Canivell and Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I don't have the August one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you got two reports now in front of you, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, you referred earlier to a report that you read and that you concluded did not contain the accurate or necessary information, and that report was written by Mr. Avlijas, and I believe you recalled it as directing its attention at least in part to Omarska. Were either of these reports the report that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you seen these reports before, or did you see these reports in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know that representatives -- a representative of the Ministry of Justice, or that Mr. Avlijas in particular, had prepared or submitted reports concerning detention facilities, prisons, or collection centres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So are you saying that at the time, you weren't -- well, what about the other Avlijas report to which you alluded, the one that you thought was inadequate and that concerned Omarska; did you see that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw that report several years later. And based on the text, I can see that it's not this report because this report says under Prijedor "No camp here," whereas I remember that the other report reflected that he had been to Omarska and described the appearance of latrines and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the witness be presented with the document contained behind tab 89, the report dated 17 August 1992 by Vojin Lale and Mirko Erkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
