utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I will certainly give you more time to look at this if you need to, but I note at page 3 of the English translation, in the second section of the report, it addresses Omarska near Prijedor and, among other things, it reports that prisoners are accommodated in a hall with military beds and clean toilet facilities. As I mentioned, feel free to look the report over if you need to, but my question is whether or not this is the report that you were referring to, although you recall it as being by Mr. Avlijas.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not this one. I remember for a fact that it was Avlijas's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when you first saw this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you turn to the first page of this report, it begins by noting that according to the decision number 0620 of the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of August 9th, 1992, that the commission for inspecting detention centres and other facilities was established. Were you familiar with that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed one such decision, perhaps this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to tab 38 which contain the minutes of the 47th session of the government. Sorry, before we actually go into that, perhaps it's helpful to show you the contents of tab 86 and ask you whether or not that was the decision that you referred to a moment ago. For the record, tab 89 [sic] contains a decision issued at the session of the government held on 9 August 1992, entitled "Decision on the Establishment of Commissions for the Inspection of Collection Centres and Other Facilities for Prisoners in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Did you sign that document for Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can look at the minutes of the government session, the 47th session of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see that you're referring to 86 and then suddenly 89 appears where --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it should be 86 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the next document, the 47th session, is contained behind tab 38. I believe that's in front of the witness now. The English translation -- the translation and I believe even the original indicate that that session was held on August 9th. I think we've already -- if you look up and see above, these would have been transcribed on the 20th, and I think we'll see another document indicating the correct date of that session, which I believe to be the 19th. In addition, it refers to the minutes of the 46th session, which was held on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now this is a session at which you were present, Mr. Trbojevic, and can I ask you to look at agenda item 7. Agenda item 7, contained at page 3 of the English translation, states that, "The government agreed on holding a special closed government session in which to discuss a report on touring of concentration centres and other detention facilities in Krajina Autonomous Region." Now, is that a reference to the report by -- that was ordered on August 9th and that was prepared by Mr. Lale and Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably one of those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the report that bears the date of 17 August 1992, submitted by Mr. Lale and Mr. Erkic, is dated a Report of the Commission for Inspecting Detention Centres and Other Facilities for Prisoners in the Autonomous Region of Krajina, so is there any reason to think this isn't the report in question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably the one because I see that, among others, Vojin Lale was also in attendance at this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is clearly the report prepared in response to the order you signed on August 9th because it states in its first sentence, "According to the decision number 06-20." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the closed session of this -- held at the same session, the 47th session, found at tab 91. Tab 91 contains the minutes of a closed session of the government of the Serbian Republic held on 19 August 1992 which, according to the minutes, was held upon the conclusion of a regular 47th government session, the minutes for which we looked at a moment ago. That session was attended by the ministers who attended the 47th government session, and that would include you, correct, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it states in item number 2: "The government discussed and adopted the commission report on the visits for collection centres and other buildings used for captives in the Autonomous Region of Krajina and assessed that the report realistically described the situation in these buildings." So my first question, Mr. Trbojevic, is: How is it that you told us that you saw this report for the first time here in court when it was discussed and adopted on the 19th of August, 1992 in your presence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me when I tell you that I don't know. I have -- I evidently saw it and discussed it on two occasions but why it was not impressed in my memory, I don't know, but according to the minutes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I would like to remind you again that if there's any fear on your behalf that you would incriminate yourself by giving the truthful answer to a question, just address us. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, enumerated item 2 states, "The government discussed and adopted the report on collection centres and other buildings used for captives in the Autonomous Region of Krajina." What people were encompassed by the word "captives" as used in the first sentence of enumerated item 2?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably refers to those about whom the report that we have before us talks about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you still have the report in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be provided to the witness. Madam Usher, could you assist? We're now talking about the report, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe it was tab 86, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, I'm sorry to interrupt, I just wanted further information about something. When would meetings be held in closed session? When would the government hold its meeting in closed session; in other words, when would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this take place, Witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were no special circumstances, it was an ordinary session, it was just held in the absence of the technical staff that usually was there at the session, but it did not mean that the public was excluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when a meeting is held in closed session, it's usually because some information is not leaked out, perhaps some employees or the public is not informed. There's a measure of precaution that is taken here. Why? You were the Deputy Prime Minister -- no, you were the deputy minister, Djeric was Prime Minister at the time. You must know why the decision was taken to hold a closed session meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assure you I don't know. There was more information in the public domain than in our reports about all these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to belabour the point, but you held quite a high position, you are a lawyer, an intelligent man; decisions like these are not taken without valid reason. This formal decision is taken after a decision has been taken. A decision to hold a meeting in closed session is something where a number of people or the public is not informed about a number of things. Could you tell me, please, why this meeting was held in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you because I do not remember the specific reason behind it. I suppose that in view of the fact that some of the reports contained accurate information that we would have to discuss it; however, these reports only said what the situation was like and that we should work to improve it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So allow me, but I would like to ask my question again. This report talked about true facts and these had to be discussed in closed session. If this reflected what was actually happening, why did this meeting have to be held in closed session? [In English] "This report talked about true facts and these had to be discussed in closed session." [Interpretation] I don't understand what connection there can be between real facts and a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not making an objection, I'm just wondering whether through Judge Hanoteau, with respect, something could be cleared up which might complement Judge Hanoteau's questions. The witness indicated that a closed session was held in the absence of technical staff, but it did not mean that the public was excluded. Your Honours, I wonder whether, as a foundation and as a complement to Judge Hanoteau's questions, the witness could be invited to make very specifically clear what happened in a normal government session that was not closed; who would be there and who wouldn't? Because the public attending a government session does strike one as a rather unusual position, and then what the difference was between a public -- an ordinary session, I'm sorry, an ordinary session and a closed session so that we can understand what was happening as the foundation for these questions. I hope that's a helpful intervention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Government sessions were mostly held at Pale and less often elsewhere. On this occasion, I believe it was in Banja Luka. It was customary for the government session to be attended by the ministers, their immediate associates, or some of those who had to present their working materials, like Mr. Lale here, because he was one of the persons involved in the drafting of the report. Closed session was quite uncustomary, we did not often resort to that form of convening, and it meant that the auxiliary staff, ministers excluded, was not supposed to be there. On this particular occasion, there was no special need for that because the material had been copied for the earlier session and was therefore there to be seen by everyone, and I simply thought that the report was going to be complemented by some information that it did not contain at this particular closed session. But I cannot tell you why it was that we turned to closed session there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I put it in a different way to you, Mr. Trbojevic. Would you agree that a closed session, whether you exclude technical staff or anyone else who would ordinarily be present, that a closed session serves to keep those who are excluded away from the conversations, positions, information discussed at such a closed session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us any specific reason why it would have been different in respect of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said that the only reason that I could conceive of would lie in the fact that the report in the form in which it had been presented could have been complemented in that -- during that session with some information that it did not previously contain. However, based on what I can read here, I don't see that anything of the sort was done. And I do not recall anyone giving any arguments or information at this session that were previously unknown to us. Because as I've said, you could find much more information in the press and on the television at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What information would you find in the press at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Photographs of people standing behind barbed wire were published. They were there, emaciated. I believe this was Trnopolje. A TV crew, either of the BBC or of some other broadcasting house, had already been there. Mr. Owen was there at Manjaca and I believe all of this happened before this session. I believe so, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that having an open session, in view of what you said about the content of the report, would have been, by far, to be preferred in order to take away this -- what you at that time thought to be a totally wrong impression of what in these detention facilities happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Trbojevic, the closed session was called to discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I lost -- out of sight that we are already at 20 minutes to 1.00. If it would not be -- if you have one question, of course you could put it and then we have to break, but if there is more to ask to the witness, then we'd like to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think breaking now is appropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn until five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, if I can follow up just a bit on a couple of questions asked by Judge Hanoteau, and I'm directing your attention to the report contained at tab 89, Permission for Inspecting Detention Centres and Other Facilities for Prisoners in the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps, Mr. Tieger, it was one of the questions: Could we check the translation in relation to concentration centres because often we -- the term is used "concentration camps," sometimes "collection centres." Could we first try to see that the language used here is properly translated from the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's an excellent suggestion, Your Honour, and I would note ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was Judge Hanoteau's suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we see that distinction in the two documents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There are a couple of ways of doing that, Your Honour. We could ask the witness to read the heading in the two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you can invite him to do so, then of course the focus, and I inform the translators, the interpreters that the focus is very much on the specific term used and if later on -- let's first see what the term is and then see whether there are any additional questions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, could you read, please, the title of the April 17th report, and if you could read that slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Report of the Commission Upon Visiting Collection Centres and Other Facilities for Prisoners in the Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are the minutes of the 47th session, that is the document found at tab 38, still in front of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document I have is from the closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Trbojevic, do you have the minutes of the open session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Read the entry at agenda item 7.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A Report Upon Visiting Collection Centres and Other Facilities for Prisoner --" it's a mistake, it should be "Prisoners in the Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It turns out, Mr. Tieger, that at least that translation on paper is not a correct one, where I did understand that it was collection centres and not concentration centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right, and I think the same can be said in -- of the title of the report. I understood it to be -- to the extent that distinction is one we need to correct, I recall it as being identified as collection centres, again in the title of the report, and it's translated as detention centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then the third source would be the -- where agenda item 7 is further elaborated upon on page 3 in the English and on page 4, first item, in the B/C/S. I don't know whether the same words are used there or not, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At this point, perhaps the most expeditious thing would be to check and see whether the words in B/C/S are precisely the same. If they're not, we can bring it to the Court's attention, but otherwise we will change the translation to conform to the interpretation in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trbojevic, returning to the report and the questions that Judge Hanoteau asked you about both the report and the opened and closed session, I just want to clarify a couple of issues. Did I understand you to indicate that you saw no reason to go into closed session because the report had already been distributed, and unless additional items beyond the contents of the report were discussed in closed session, there wouldn't be any need for that, there didn't seem to be any need for that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, agenda item 7, if I recall it correctly, said, "That the government agreed to hold a special closed session to discuss the report." Does that indicate that the report was not discussed in the open session but that the discussion about the report took place in the closed session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that now. That was 12 or 13 years ago, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The report itself is a -- bears the heading "top classified." What kind of documents were issued the designation "top classified" at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were regulations, mostly in the domain of the military administration, which specified what and under what circumstances can be considered a confidential document or confidential action. Now, who it was who decided to put this strictly confidential designation on this document and why that was done, I couldn't tell you that now. The contents of the minutes from that session does not justify the treatment this document received as a strictly confidential one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again interrupt for one second, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Trbojevic, before the break, you explained to us that you couldn't understand why such a session would be a closed session because the report was distributed beforehand and what you heard during this closed session where you expected, perhaps, to have some addition to the report, that you didn't hear anything new. Now after the break, you're telling us that you did not know whether the report was discussed in closed session or whether it was discussed in open session. Because that was the question put to you by

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Does that indicate that the report was not discussed in the open session but that the discussion about the report took place in the closed session?" After the answers you have given before the break, is your answer that you couldn't say because it was 12 or 13 years ago is a correct one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I said that if the minutes reflected that the report was discussed, then it is obvious that we did discuss it, that we held it in our hands. As for the extent to which it was discussed, I really don't know. Now, whether, in the closed session, we continued this debate, whether we tried to expand it, I really don't know. The definite fact is that it was a topic on -- in both instances, but to what extent we discussed it on the first occasion and on the second occasion, this is something that I couldn't tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, I asked you earlier about an entry in the minutes of the closed session that indicates the government discussed and adopted the report on the visit to collection centres and other buildings used for captives in the autonomous region. I asked you what was embraced by the term "captives," and I believe that you said -- you believed it to be those persons who were the subject of the report. Can I ask you to turn then to page 6 of the English translation, and it's item 5 of the conclusions of the report. It states, "There are no regulations regarding the way civilian refugees are treated, and this problem was especially emphasised in Trnopolje." It's actually written apparently as something else but it's seen by the interpreter as possibly Trnopolje. First of all, perhaps you can clarify that for us. Does that item refer to Trnopolje in particular? Is that the word used there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to item 5, in my version it's on page 6 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness gave the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and it says here, "Lack of appropriate regulations on how to treat civilian population who had become refugees, which is particularly evident --" it says here "in Tromolje," but in most likelihood it should be Trnopolje. Is that what you asked me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And what did you understand to be the impact of the absence of regulations on the civilians who were held in -- or who were gathered in or who were contained in collection centres or other buildings, as referred to in item 2 of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report under item 1 has a heading Trnopolje near Prijedor, and in there, it says that this centre is of an open nature, meaning that anybody can enter it or leave to go to the place they desire to go to, that certain documentation needs to be provided and so on. Therefore, the information circulated was that the collection centre was the place where people sought shelter, people fleeing from war operations. It was also said that allegedly people in charge of their security were protecting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them there. This was the information received and used, and this is partially what is reflected here in the report. I know that the government passed a decree on ensuring proper treatment for refugees. I know that there was a bill on refugees that was worked on, but I don't know what the final solution was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware, at that time, of allegations, either in the international media, by NGOs, by government representatives, that persons gathered in Trnopolje camp had been forcibly driven from their homes, many of which had been destroyed by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of that naturally was contained in the information we received. Now, as to when those facts reached us, I couldn't really tell you. And even today, it is difficult to assess the authenticity of that information, or the accuracy of that information. However, it is a fact that after significant military operations in certain areas, after the troops had passed, in their wake, there were villages and towns that were destroyed and that there were many citizens who needed to be taken care of. Some of them were taken care of in Trnopolje, according to the information that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And how did you determine when -- what information did you receive to verify the fact that after significant military operations, villages and towns were destroyed and many people were rendered homeless?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke about these reports and that was the first, the initial information. Afterwards, in the media, much more was reported, and then later, a lot more surfaced. Now, as to the chronology of the events, exactly when I heard what, I don't think that I could be able to tell you that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not looking for specific dates, but let me ask you this: Are you saying that this report represents the first occasion on which you learned that military operations had resulted in the displacement of large numbers of people, and specifically Muslims, from their homes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that question, truly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not kept abreast of the military operations. I didn't know what took place in which theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, it emerged that parts of villages, settlements were destroyed, burned down, the same applied for roads, that the population was gone. Therefore, I don't know how to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know before receiving this report that Bosnian Serb forces were -- viewed themselves as being in control of 65 to 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This piece of information was used in conducting the political campaign. The percentages were circulated and used. Now, as to how much of that was accurate, I don't think that anybody would be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, did you hear that from the leadership of Republika Srpska? That is, did you hear that from either Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik or both?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Karadzic mentioned these percentages several times, these ownership percentages before the war and then the percentages of the territory controlled by the respective parties. I believed I heard it from him on several occasions. But this could also be found in the press, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you understand that to encompass municipalities in the areas in which Muslims had been a majority before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, during peace negotiations, it became quite clear that any peace-making process entailed that some of the territories held by certain sides should be given over to the control of the other side, including the settlements in these areas. This was a matter of a debate that was largely in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, that was not the question. The question was: Did you understand that -- and that is the territory expressed in percentages controlled by Bosnian Serb forces, did you understand that to encompass municipalities in the areas in which Muslims had been a majority before the outbreak of the conflict? So whether control also included territories where there was majority Muslim population before the outbreak of the conflict. That was the question, not how you negotiated later on and whether matters should be changed. That's what you were asked by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've quite understood and there's no doubt about it but I did not understand it from these reports from the government sessions held on the 17th of August and the 18th of August, and that's what we are discussing it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you understood it, didn't you, from your discussions with other officials in the Bosnian Serb authorities, from your attendance at Assembly sessions, from your general contact with people at a high level of politics within Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every Assembly session was opened with the report on the political situation and on the situation in the theatres of war, and this report was often submitted by President Karadzic and often times by General Mladic whenever he was attending the session, and then you could hear the state of affairs with regard to the peace negotiating process and with regard to the military situation, actions on Igman, at Gorazde, and so on and so forth. This information was something that you were unable to follow closely unless you had a map in front of you to be able to follow the movements of the respective units. But you are given the information and you take notice of it, and that's it. You're not able to respond to that in terms of saying to a general that they -- that he made a wrong decision at some point. This was beyond our power. We were unable to tell Karadzic, for instance, why he advocated a certain position at this and this negotiating meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Trbojevic, the only question put to you is from -- how you learned that areas under the control of the Bosnian Serb forces also included areas where there was a majority Muslim population before the conflict. You are telling us a lot. You're not answering the question. Because the last time Mr. Tieger put it to you, you said -- when you said that you did not understand it from these reports, then Mr. Tieger asked you, "You understood it, didn't you, from your discussion with other officials, from your attendance at Assembly sessions, from your general contact with people at a high level of politics within Republika Srpska." The only thing Mr. Tieger is asking you, how did you learn that? And not whether you could comment on it, whether you could criticise it; that's how did you learn that there was military control by Bosnian Serb forces over areas which had a majority Muslim population before the conflict broke out. You told us that you were in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just answered that question. The report on both the political situation and the war operations was submitted to the Assembly session and one could hear a lot of information from these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So on the basis of that, you would know where there was military control over a territory. Yes? In general terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you know who was the majority population through these discussions or did you know that by any other means, or was it common knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was more or less common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You got the military reports, you had knowledge about what was the majority population, and that's the basis of your knowledge. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm hesitant to leave this subject but there's one thing I want to cover before we break, if I may. Can the report contained at tab 92 be presented to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, this is a report we looked at earlier when we were trying to -- when I was asking you to determine whether or not it was the Avlijas report that you had referred to, and I believe you indicated it was not. This report deals with Trebinje, Gacko, and Bileca with SAO Herzegovina, and as you note, at the bottom it is signed by Slobodan Avlijas and Goran Saric. Can you tell us when you first saw this report, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to provide the witness with the governments -- the minutes of the government session of September 7th, 1992 contained at tab 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is another session at which you were present, Mr. Trbojevic. And can I ask you to turn your attention to agenda item 15.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That indicates that, "A government commissioned report on a tour of camps --" here it says, "concentration centres." That may well be "collection centres," we'll have that checked -- "in SAO Herzegovina was adopted." Is that a reference to the report of Mr. Avlijas and Mr. Saric found at tab 92?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if you look at the top of the report itself, it contains in handwriting DD 15, or presumed to be agenda 15. And then it says, "Received August 22nd, 1992," and it bears a number.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it means, but it does say that it was received on the 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, doesn't it mean that this is the report referred to, in fact, in agenda item 15, and isn't it clear that this particular copy of the report was used in that session, or intended for that session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Trbojevic, with respect, of course I know it's possible but I'm asking you if there's any reason to dispute the conclusion I've just reached that this report, this copy of the report that bears the designation number 15 that corresponds to agenda item 15 in the minutes of the 49th session of September 7th, correspond. If so, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reason to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It appears that Mr. Avlijas and Mr. Saric reported back on their findings in Trebinje, Gacko, and Bileca, finding that in Trebinje there is no camp; that Bileca there are two detention centres, one of which had no prisoners because all the prisoners had been exchanged the day before; that there were 140 Muslims in another facility in Bileca; and that there were no prisoners in Gacko. Can you tell us about any discussion you remember at the government session on September 7th about the -- about this report and about its relative accuracy or thoroughness or anything else about the report that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN TRBOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can address one more report but we've gone over the last time, and perhaps I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, we'll continue tomorrow but in the afternoon in this same courtroom, at a quarter past 2.00. I again would like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony you have been giving. We'd like to hear from you tomorrow morning whether there was anything wrong in the transcript of the interview that was presented to you, whether there's anything we should check on the basis of the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness received that yesterday, if it's possible to check with him today, maybe we could undertake a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, did you have an opportunity to review the transcript pages that were given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there anything which was not correct which we have to check on the basis of the audio recording?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for that. I believe it's been transcribed quite accurately. We were talking about a decision that in my opinion derogated the constitution, and then when we came to the decision whereby the War Presidency was expanded, then it suddenly turns out as if I had said that this decision was the most important one. Well, I said yes, it was, because it shows the gravest form of violation of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We heard your evidence on it. If there are any further questions to be put to you in relation to that pages, they will be put to you either by the Prosecution or Defence. The main reason why we gave you the transcript was in order to give you an opportunity to verify whether the transcript was a correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, has the witness had the whole transcript or just selected pages? I'm unclear about that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we discussed that yesterday, that Mr. Tieger was hesitant to give him only a couple of pages. The Chamber then decided that if any the parties --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if any of the parties would like to give him more, fine, but most important for the Chamber at that moment was that an opportunity would be given to the witness where he specifically commented on the correctness of the transcript to at least give him the smaller context. But if anyone would like to give him more, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for reminding me about that. Yes, the Defence would request -- it's 130 pages overall, but it is, after all, an interview with -- was an interview with him. We'd request that he has the whole thing, because for cross-examination, I can't know which pages I might decide are useful for one reason or another to put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a suggestion. If it needs any discussion at this moment, I'd rather do it in the absence of the witness. And Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Trbojevic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the suggestion by the Defence is that the whole of the interviews would be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I disagree with that, Your Honour. This is a taped interview. We've discussed it at length with the witness and in the course of his testimony, with respect to one small issue a question arose about the accuracy of the transcription. He had a chance to review it now. He said that it was accurate. If such a circumstance arises again, and based on our -- based upon the experience thus far in using a transcript, I don't think that's likely to happen. We can address it at that time. But I see no reason otherwise to depart from the customary practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's hard to see, in the Defence's submission, why the Prosecution is so resistant to this. The -- first of all, the transcript itself indicates in a number of -- at a number of points that it's perhaps not 100 per cent reliable. That's apparent on its face. Why the witness should not -- should not have that simple opportunity of reviewing the whole of his own statement and alerting or being prepared to alert the Trial Chamber quickly and efficiently as to any difficulties is hard to understand. What is it that the Prosecution is so concerned about in allowing this witness simply to read a statement -- a transcript of his own interview, which presumably he was supplied with a long time ago anyway?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission, the witness has said nothing that indicates his interest in doing so, desire to do so, or need to do so. This is Mr. Stewart's submission, not the submission of the witness and the witness seemed to have no difficult proceeding the way we've been proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's no indication the witness has refused to do it. He would do it if requested, we feel quite confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the request of the Defence. The Chamber has observed -- [B/C/S on English channel] I received the B/C/S, but I'm back on English again. The Chamber has observed that the witness seems to be not without difficulties in knowing exactly what his recollection is and it could not be excluded that apart from relying on what he still remembers, that he is also selective in what he remembers. Providing him with the statement he gave as a suspect might contribute to the difficulties the witness may face as I just explained. Therefore, the application is denied. One thing I would like to raise in the absence of the witness, because although it has got nothing to do with him, is as far as recalling Mr. Bjelobrk as a witness for cross-examination, I do understand that no final agreement has been reached in every respect by the Prosecution and Defence and it's -- we are still waiting for the Defence to give its final position on what subjects they would insist on recalling Mr. Bjelobrk for further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we know that by not later than by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wonder if -- Your Honour, the position is, frankly, I'm overwhelmed with things to do, including preparation of two witnesses this week, Your Honour. The end of this week is, I'm afraid yet again, despite the fact that time has run on, the end of this week is a very tall order. It's I who have to do this, Your Honour, it's not something I can delegate any further, and Your Honour, we are simply under enormous pressure, so may I request a little more time than that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much more time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have Mr. Kljuic coming up on Monday and Tuesday and he's a witness that I can't avoid doing because I was the one who examined him before, so Your Honour, I wonder if I might ask for the end of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the matter has been thoroughly discussed between the parties so I have some difficulties in understanding why the Defence at this moment could not identify those specific issues on which it would like to cross-examine -- further cross-examine Mr. Bjelobrk, but we'll consider it, but I'm not promising that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I say, Your Honour, the matter has been discussed but it was discussed a long time ago, and refreshment -- I made my position plain a long time ago, but refreshment of one's mind and reference to files is important, and I informed Your Honour that Ms. Cmeric also needed to look at quite a lot of material that came from Mr. Krajisnik, so that isn't something which I had dealt with before, and that is the sort of thing that I have to revisit in order to make decisions and make submissions in relation to this matter. It's considerably more time consuming and onerous than perhaps Your Honour might have appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider your request for more time and we'll let you know not later than by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
